extracted.intended_audience: US patent applicants (or their counsel) responding to European Examiner objections under the EPC
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing a response to a European Patent Office (EPO) objection under Article 56 EPC (lack of inventive step) using the EPO problem–solution approach: how to select closest prior art, formulate the objective technical problem, identify technical effects, and argue non-obviousness. Includes drafting tips for the description and recommended response wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art is the most realistic starting point for reaching the invention. The overriding criterion is that it pertains to the same technical field and aims to solve the same or a similar technical problem as the invention. This generally means a prior art document which has a similar objective and requires the smallest number of modifications to reach the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opinion accompanying the Search Report as a starting point. Do not choose a document merely because it shares many technical features if it does not belong to the same field or aim to solve the same problem (examples: battery cooling vs unrelated fields; yogurts vs cheeses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ex post facto considerations when selecting closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex post facto considerations should be avoided in the determination of the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document which does not mention the problem to be solved would not normally qualify as the closest prior art, regardless of the number of technical features it may have in common with the claimed invention. Do not rely on hindsight to identify a document as the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the closest prior art and the claimed invention to identify differences between the two, then identify the technical effect of those differences. The technical effect is the technical advantage provided specifically by the differences. This technical effect is used to determine the objective technical problem solved by the invention, starting from the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: if the difference is a valve in a cooling circuit, the technical effect might be improved control over coolant flow, leading to better battery temperature control; the objective technical problem would be framed as 'how to improve temperature control of a battery?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and associate technical effects to claim features in the description
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting the description, be careful to associate a technical effect to each of the features found in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly linking features to technical effects in the description will help defend any feature in the problem–solution approach during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate inventive step by considering whether the skilled person would be prompted to modify the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether there is any teaching in the rest of the prior art or in the closest prior art itself that would have prompted the skilled person, whose goal is to solve the objective technical problem, to modify or adapt the closest prior art to reach the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions of strength: (a) if none of the prior art documents provide solutions for solving the objective technical problem (e.g., none discuss a valve for coolant flow), you are in a strong position to defend inventive step; (b) if cited prior art discusses the objective technical problem but solves it with a different solution, you can also defend inventive step; (c) if prior art describes the same solution but not for solving the same technical problem, you should still be able to contest lack of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument from difference-in-purpose (same feature disclosed for a different purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the missing feature is disclosed in the prior art but for a different purpose, then you will have a solid argument to defend the inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that the prior art's disclosure of a feature for a different technical purpose does not render the claimed solution obvious for the objective technical problem at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to an Article 56 EPC objection by explicitly following the problem–solution approach
rubrics_metrics.description: When replying to an objection under Article 56 EPC, you should respond by clearly following the problem–solution approach and clearly stating each step of the approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong response includes explicit phrasing such as: 'The difference between document D1 and the claim is [...]', 'the technical effect of this difference is [...]', 'the objective technical problem is [...]', 'none of the cited prior art discloses the claimed solution for solving the objective technical problem' or 'Document D2 discloses a solution which is different to the claimed solution'. Such explicit wording is more likely to convince an examiner that the claimed invention is inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow EPO law and guidelines (Article 56 EPC; EPO guideline G‑VII‑5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step assessments should be grounded in Article 56 EPC and the EPO's problem–solution guidance (EPO guideline G‑VII‑5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame arguments to align with the problem–solution approach as described in EPO practice and cite the legal/guideline authority where appropriate.
